dailyBrief.text: Good morning, Smileys — and a big welcome to Benji, who arrived this weekend after Saturday night's hospital trip. It is a cloudy, mild Monday in Solon, high near 64°, with no rain expected and the first early sunset of standard time at 5:19 tonight. Overnight, Iran left the Doha talks with a draft U.S. deal circulating that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the naval blockade ends, while Senator Chris Murphy was hospitalized after a stroke at his son's hockey game, with a full recovery expected. There is no early voting today, so tomorrow is the day: polls are open 6:30 AM to 7:30 PM for the midterms, and 66 Cuyahoga County precincts — including some in Solon — have new polling places, so check yours before you go. Tonight's home entertainment is set too, with the Cavs hosting Oklahoma City at Rocket Arena at 7 PM.

items.title: Cavs vs Oklahoma City Thunder
Oil falls as Doha talks produce a draft and a two-day plan to reopen Hormuz
items.summary:
Oil prices dropped sharply on Monday as a third straight day of talks in Doha raised hopes that shipping through the Strait of Hormuz could resume quickly. Iranian negotiators have finished that run of meetings with Qatari mediators and a draft proposal is now circulating, with a follow-up meeting possible. Brent was reported down more than 3% in early trading.

Under the version Tehran is putting forward, measures by Washington on a first day would be followed by a reopening of the strait on a second day. That compresses an earlier seven-step Iranian plan from September. The demands attached to it remain broad, covering sanctions relief and oil waivers, an end to the naval blockade, frozen assets, a smaller U.S. military presence, and an end to fighting on other fronts.

The market move is about expectations, not restored supply. Major gaps remain on Iran's nuclear program and on sanctions and security, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said President Trump has not decided on new strikes and would prefer a diplomatic outcome. Until Washington publicly answers the draft, energy prices are likely to stay sensitive to each headline.

Watch for a U.S. response to the draft, any date for a follow-up meeting, and whether tanker traffic actually changes. A deal on shipping alone would not settle the nuclear dispute.

items.title: Bulgaria elects Iliana Iotova as its first elected female president
items.summary:
Acting President Iliana Iotova has won Bulgaria's presidential runoff, according to near-final results released Monday. With almost all precinct protocols counted, her ticket had about 57.6% of the vote, well ahead of former caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov at about 39.5%.

The runoff followed an October 25 first round in which no ticket won a majority. Iotova had taken over as acting president in January after Rumen Radev resigned, and she ran with backing that included Radev's allies and the Bulgarian Socialist Party. Turnout was low in both rounds, and a small share of voters chose the option supporting no one.

The result puts the presidency and the government in allied hands when her full term begins in January 2027, giving Prime Minister Rumen Radev a political boost. The presidency is largely ceremonial, but it still carries weight in appointments, foreign representation, and moments of government crisis.

The election commission still needs to formally confirm the final result. Attention will then turn to how closely the presidency and government coordinate, and whether low turnout prompts a wider debate about public disengagement.

items.title: U.N. peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara ends after 35 years
items.summary:
The United Nations mission in Western Sahara, known as MINURSO, has ceased operations after 35 years. Its mandate expired at midnight on Saturday after the Security Council failed to agree on an extension, and Sunday marked the start of a liquidation phase.

The mission was created in 1991 to monitor a ceasefire and prepare a referendum on self-determination that never took place. The end came after Russia vetoed a U.S. draft resolution and a rival Russian proposal to extend the mission failed to win enough votes. A smaller U.N. team will now oversee moving equipment and assets back to contributing countries.

Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said the U.N. still stands ready to support talks through his personal envoy, Staffan de Mistura, and that ending the mission does not remove the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination. Morocco welcomed the outcome, while the Algeria-backed Polisario Front expressed concern.

Without peacekeepers on the ground, there is less independent monitoring if tensions rise along the berm that divides the territory. The next test is whether diplomacy without MINURSO can keep the long-frozen conflict from becoming active again.

items.title: Ukraine resumes refinery strikes as U.S. floats returning Russian gas to Europe
items.summary:
Ukraine has resumed long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries, with reports of hits in the Nizhny Novgorod region and in Samara in recent days. The renewed campaign comes despite earlier U.S. pressure on Kyiv to pause attacks on energy infrastructure.

At the same time, a Wall Street Journal report says U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff raised an idea in September to restart Russian gas sales to Europe through Ukraine, using a U.S. intermediary. Under the concept, Ukraine would earn transit revenue, some Russian proceeds could be held in escrow, and an energy ceasefire could be pursued before winter. Transit through Ukraine stopped at the end of 2024 when the old contract was not renewed.

European opposition is a major obstacle. EU law requires an end to Russian gas imports by the end of 2027, and the EU energy commissioner has rejected a return to reliance on Moscow. Reuters said it could not immediately verify the Journal report, and no government has publicly confirmed the proposal as settled policy — treat this as a reported proposal, not a confirmed deal.

If mid-November three-way talks go ahead, energy targets and gas transit are expected to be central. Continued refinery strikes and Russian attacks on Ukraine's grid would raise pressure for a ceasefire while also making any gas arrangement harder to sell.

items.title: France opens attempted-murder probe after petrol bomb attack on police in Paris
items.summary:
Paris prosecutors have opened an attempted-murder investigation after incendiary devices were thrown at security forces at the end of a demonstration on Saturday. About 15 gendarmes and police officers were targeted at Porte de Charenton, and images showed a device exploding at an officer's feet and setting protective gear alight.

Prosecutors said reported injuries included second-degree burns and tinnitus, though the full assessment was still provisional. No one had been arrested specifically over that attack at the time of reporting. Separately, the Interior Ministry put nationwide arrests during the demonstrations and Halloween night at 779, including 105 in Paris.

The march was part of a third weekend of protests focused on high living costs and government policies. Officials said the overall arrest total was lower than on the previous two weekends, even as the firebomb incident drew condemnation from Interior Minister Laurent Nunez and political leaders.

Investigators now need to identify who threw the devices. How the case proceeds, and whether the next demonstrations stay peaceful, will shape the government's response to a protest movement that has not yet faded.

items.title: More than 200 arrested in Germany after youth protests turn violent overnight
items.summary:
Largely peaceful daytime marches by young people in more than 30 German cities on Saturday were followed by overnight clashes in Frankfurt, Berlin, Hamburg, and Cologne. German media and police reports put arrests and detentions nationwide at more than 200 by early Sunday.

Frankfurt saw the worst damage, with shop windows smashed and at least five shops looted, more than 100 officers injured there according to Hesse authorities, and dozens arrested. Berlin police reported up to 56 people detained and 27 officers injured, while Hamburg took about 120 people into custody after burning barricades were set up near the central bus station. Police also used water cannon in Cologne.

The marches, organized under the name Gen Z regelt, focused on living costs, underfunded education, cuts to public services, and opposition to reviving compulsory military service. Organizers distanced themselves from the violence, disputed claims that extremists had infiltrated the Frankfurt march, and announced another nationwide demonstration for November 14.

The contrast between the daytime rallies and the overnight unrest is now the political problem for both organizers and authorities. The November 14 turnout and whether it stays peaceful will be the immediate measure.

items.title: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to set aside 20,000 California ballots on eve of election
items.summary:
The Trump administration filed an emergency request with the Supreme Court on Monday asking it to stop California from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters unless their citizenship is first verified. The Justice Department wants those ballots separated from other votes in the November 3 midterms.

The list came from the Department of Homeland Security and was sent to state and Los Angeles County officials. A district judge rejected the administration's request on October 28, and the 9th Circuit refused it on Friday, warning that using the list could block valid votes and jeopardize the Los Angeles County election. California says its safeguards are robust and that the federal method for building the list is flawed.

The case tests how far the executive branch can go in state-run elections, which the Constitution assigns mainly to states and Congress. Legal experts quoted in coverage called the filing an extraordinary, last-minute remedy, especially with voting already underway and Election Day one day away.

The Supreme Court could act quickly or let the lower-court rulings stand for this election. Either way, with California holding 52 House seats, the decision could affect closely watched House races and set a precedent for future federal challenges to state voter lists.

items.title: Trump says he would preemptively pardon Elon Musk and aides if needed
items.summary:
President Trump said in a New York Post podcast interview aired Monday that he would consider preemptive pardons for Elon Musk and other White House aides if he thought they needed protection. He was asked about the prospect of House Democrats investigating or trying to arrest Musk if they win power.

Trump said he would not hesitate if he decided pardons were necessary, comparing the idea to pardons issued by President Joe Biden before leaving office. A preemptive pardon in this context would be issued before any formal charge. Musk is a close ally who spent heavily to support Trump in 2024 and, according to the New York Times figures cited in coverage, has spent $474 million to help Republicans in the 2026 midterms.

The remarks land because Democrats are favored to take the House in Tuesday's vote, which would give them control of investigative committees. Coverage notes Democrats have signaled possible inquiries into Musk's time leading the Department of Government Efficiency, his companies' federal contracts, and Starlink decisions related to Ukraine.

No pardon has been issued on this basis, and the comments do not name specific alleged offenses. Watch whether Trump repeats the pledge after the results, and whether House control actually changes hands.

items.title: Stevens fallout deepens: Michigan party cuts ties, Jeffries flags caucus discussion, El-Sayed raises millions in hours
items.summary:
The fallout from Rep. Haley Stevens endorsing Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's Senate race escalated on Monday. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Stevens had made a terrible decision and that House Democrats will discuss appropriate next steps when they return, while Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel said Stevens is no longer a member of the state party.

Stevens appeared with Rogers at a Detroit church on Sunday, endorsing him over Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed after losing to El-Sayed in the August primary. Her chief of staff and communications director resigned, several colleagues described the move as a betrayal, and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer used the same language publicly. Stevens said she was not turning her back on Democrats and pointed to El-Sayed's associations and a disputed pro-El-Sayed ad as reasons for her break.

The immediate electoral effect ran the other way in fundraising: El-Sayed's campaign reported raising $1.2 million in four hours after the endorsement, described as its second-best fundraising stretch since securing the nomination, and USA Today's live coverage put the total raised since the endorsement at $2.4 million by Monday morning. That surge suggests the endorsement mobilized El-Sayed supporters at least as much as it helped Rogers.

Michigan is one of the closest Senate races in the country and could help decide control of the chamber. Any formal caucus action against Stevens would come after Election Day, but the race itself will show on Tuesday whether the endorsement moved persuadable voters or mainly hardened both camps.

items.title: Final Senate polls put Democrats ahead in all seven battlegrounds, with most races still close
items.summary:
A final round of New York Times and Siena University polls released ahead of Election Day puts Democratic Senate candidates numerically ahead in all seven battleground states surveyed: Michigan, Texas, Maine, Ohio, Kansas, Alaska, and Iowa. The surveys were conducted October 23 to November 1 among 5,708 likely voters.

The largest leads were in Michigan, where Abdul El-Sayed led Mike Rogers 53% to 42%, and Texas, where James Talarico led Ken Paxton 50% to 43%. Troy Jackson led Susan Collins 51% to 45% in Maine, Sherrod Brown led Jon Husted 49% to 44% in Ohio, and Adam Hamilton led Roger Marshall 49% to 44% in Kansas. Alaska and Iowa were within the margins of error, at 48% to 46% and 48% to 47% respectively.

USA Today's summary stresses that Democrats led in five of the seven when margins of error are taken into account, and Republicans including Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson disputed the picture while campaigning in Iowa. Across the seven states, only 38% of likely voters approved of Trump's job performance in the poll, even though he carried five of those states by double digits in 2024. The Michigan poll was also taken before the Stevens endorsement of Rogers.

Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take the Senate. Poll leads on the eve of voting are not results — turnout, late deciders, and polling response differences noted by the Times itself could still swing several of these races either way on Tuesday.

items.title: Republicans pour late money into normally safe Senate seats in Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi
items.summary:
Republicans are spending tens of millions of dollars in last-minute advertising to defend Senate seats in Kansas, South Carolina, and Mississippi, according to Axios reporting summarized on Monday. Those are states the party would normally expect to hold without a rescue effort.

The report says the three incumbents or nominees were warned for months that their campaigns were in danger and did not respond strongly enough, forcing national Republicans to divert resources. That diversion matters because the same money and attention could otherwise go to the seven toss-up races that will decide the Senate majority.

Kansas is already on the battleground list in final polling, with Democrat Adam Hamilton leading Sen. Roger Marshall. Expanding the defensive map to South Carolina and Mississippi suggests Republican strategists see risk beyond the states both parties have contested all cycle.

If Democrats remain competitive in normally safe Republican territory, even losing narrowly there can strain the GOP across the map. Tuesday's margins in those three states will show whether the late spending steadied the races or whether the warning signs were broader than the toss-ups.

items.title: Sen. Chris Murphy is awake and alert after stroke, office says, with no newer update Monday morning
items.summary:
Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut is awake and alert and responding well to treatment at Johns Hopkins after suffering a stroke on Saturday, his office said in its Sunday statement. As of Monday morning, his office had not released a newer update, according to local coverage summarizing that statement.

Chief of staff Allison Herwitt said Murphy first felt numbness in his arm while at his son's hockey game on Saturday afternoon. He was taken to a local hospital, where doctors determined he had had a stroke, and he was then transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring.

Herwitt said doctors are encouraged by his progress and that the office is optimistic he will make a full recovery. The statement did not give the type or severity of the stroke, how long he is expected to stay in the hospital, or when he might return to work.

Murphy, 53, has represented Connecticut in the Senate since 2013. Any further medical detail or return timeline will need to come from his office — there is no verified update beyond the Sunday statement in the reporting available at midday Monday.

items.title: Stocks climb at midday as oil drops sharply on Iran diplomacy hopes
items.summary:
Wall Street was solidly higher late Monday morning, extending the morning bounce into a broader rally. As of 11:31 a.m. ET, the Dow was up about 1.1% to 52,314, the S&P 500 was up about 0.6% to 7,629, and the Nasdaq was up about 0.8% to 25,631, with gold also rising and the 10-year Treasury yield easing slightly.

The main new driver since the open was energy. Crude fell more than 7% during the session, with Brent dropping to just under $106 a barrel and U.S. crude sliding below $100, as traders reacted to signs that Washington and Tehran might give talks more time. ExxonMobil shares fell about 2% alongside oil, while most other sectors moved higher.

Cheaper oil eases one of the inflation pressures that has weighed on voters and markets through the Iran conflict, which is why a diplomatic headline could move stocks so quickly. The move also shows how sensitive the market remains to any change in the war outlook on the eve of the midterms.

Watch Tuesday's election results, the rest of this week's earnings, and the October jobs report later in the week for whether the calmer mood holds.

items.title: Oracle seeks $20 billion in stock and bond sales to pay for its AI build-out
items.summary:
Oracle filed Monday to raise $20 billion, split between $10 billion in new common stock and $10 billion in bonds, to help fund its large AI and cloud infrastructure program. Its shares fell roughly 5% to 6% in Monday trading, adding to a decline of about a third so far this year through Friday.

The company said the money is for general purposes that can include capital spending, debt repayment, acquisitions, dividends and buybacks. The bond portion is planned in six pieces maturing between 2029 and 2046, with pricing and final share counts not yet set. Oracle carried about $125 billion in notes and other borrowings as of August 31, compared with about $67 billion in revenue for fiscal 2026.

Investors are focused on the scale and the risk. Oracle is aiming for revenue above $225 billion by fiscal 2030 and says spending will peak this fiscal year and next, while also pledging that this $20 billion is the limit for added AI financing through fiscal 2030. Unlike larger cloud rivals, Oracle has heavy exposure to OpenAI, so the market is testing whether the future revenue justifies the debt and dilution.

Watch the final pricing of both sales and whether buyers demand higher yields, which would signal how much confidence lenders have in the plan.

items.title: Amazon rebounds more than 4% as analysts focus on fast-growing cloud business
items.summary:
Amazon shares rose more than 4% by late Monday morning, recovering part of last week's post-earnings slide. The stock was up about 4.6% around 11:52 a.m. ET after rising as much as 5.6% earlier in the session.

The immediate spark was an upgrade. Phillip Securities raised Amazon to a buy rating and lifted its price target to $330 from $320, pointing to strong visibility for demand at Amazon Web Services. AWS revenue grew about 39% in the third quarter to roughly $46 billion, its fastest pace in nearly five years, and its backlog of contracted work was reported at $578 billion.

That cloud strength is competing with real concerns in the same earnings report. Amazon missed slightly on overall revenue and earnings, said capital spending would reach about $220 billion in 2026, and showed negative free cash flow of about $42 billion over the past year because of the data-center build-out.

The debate for investors is whether AWS growth stays strong enough, for long enough, to pay back that spending. Holiday retail results and advertising growth will be the next tests.

items.title: Palantir faces a high bar tonight: even about 85% growth may not be enough
items.summary:
Palantir reports its third-quarter results after the market closes Monday, and expectations are unusually demanding. Analysts expect roughly $2.18 billion in revenue, up about 85% from a year earlier, and earnings of about $0.41 a share, nearly double the year-ago figure. The company itself had guided revenue to about $2.16 billion.

In other words, a simple beat may not settle the argument. Investors want to see that U.S. commercial customers are signing enough new contract value to replace work as it converts to revenue, and that margins hold up while growth stays high. In the prior quarter, U.S. commercial contract value rose sharply and the company reported a 47% operating margin.

Valuation is the reason the bar is so high. Palantir entered the report valued at more than $440 billion, after falling about 6% on Friday to $184.11 and pulling back from a record near $213. At that price, soft guidance could matter more than a strong quarter that is already expected.

Watch the company's outlook for the fourth quarter and the full year, plus any guidance on U.S. commercial demand, when results arrive after the close. No results had been released as of midday.

items.title: Bitcoin holds near $78,000 as Binance reopens withdrawals after record $6.3 billion hack
items.summary:
Bitcoin traded near $78,000 on Monday, up about 1% and posting a third straight day of gains, despite the largest crypto exchange hack on record last week. Bitcoin had fallen about 4% on Friday to roughly $77,400 after Binance disclosed that about $6.3 billion in customer assets had been taken.

Binance began restoring withdrawals in phases over the weekend, starting with bitcoin. Customers pulled a net $3.64 billion on the first day withdrawals resumed, according to the exchange, and Binance said it had replaced about 90% to 95% of the stolen funds from its own reserves, with figures varying by update. U.S. spot bitcoin funds still saw about $643 million in outflows on Friday.

The contained price reaction is the story. A failure of this size at the world's largest exchange did not trigger the kind of broad panic selling seen in earlier crypto crises, in part because Binance moved quickly to say customers would be covered. Traders still paid more for protection against a drop, a sign nerves have not fully settled.

Watch whether withdrawals continue smoothly this week and whether fund flows recover, alongside Tuesday's midterms and Friday's jobs report, which could shape crypto regulation and risk appetite.

items.title: Apple sets dates for AI features in China, using Alibaba's Qwen in Siri and Writing Tools
items.summary:
Apple has set a concrete schedule for bringing its first Apple Intelligence features to iPhone users in mainland China. Developer testing starts with the iOS beta on November 4, and the public rollout is planned for December alongside iOS 27.3. That is separate from Apple's earnings report tonight — this is a product rollout, not a financial result.

Inside China, the experience will look different from other countries. Alibaba's Qwen model will be available through Siri, Writing Tools and Visual Intelligence for tasks such as understanding text and images and generating content. The integration is opt-in, and Alibaba says requests and responses will not be used to train its models.

The first release covers supported models including the iPhone 15 Pro line, iPhone 16 and later models, iPhone Air and iPhone Duo, in English or Simplified Chinese. It does not include the newer Siri AI or other next-generation features announced earlier this year, and support for Apple's other platforms still needs further approvals.

For Apple, China is both a major iPhone market and a regulatory test of running AI features through a local partner. Watch developer feedback after November 4 and whether the December date holds.

items.title: NTSB opens its Learjet crash investigation in Florida, as families begin naming the nine victims
items.summary:
Federal investigators began their on-site work in earnest on Monday at the Greenacres, Florida intersection where a Learjet 60 crashed on Sunday, killing all nine people aboard. The jet, flying from Austin, Texas to the Bahamas, went down at Military Trail and Cresthaven Boulevard at about 12:50 p.m. and exploded on impact, scattering debris across a busy crossroads. Governor Ron DeSantis said it fell, in his words, like a missile.

New details emerged about who was aboard and what the jet flew into. A family statement identified a co-pilot as 20-year-old Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras of Boca Raton, though authorities have not yet formally confirmed the names of those aboard. Meteorologists reviewing flight data and radar said the jet flew into a fast-growing thunderstorm whose clouds shot up 15,000 feet in 20 minutes and reached about 48,300 feet by the time of the crash; minutes earlier, the crew had asked to climb, citing more precipitation ahead.

The crash's footprint is displacing a neighborhood, not just closing a road. County Commissioner Joel Flores said about 100 homes near the site have been evacuated, displacing an estimated 400 to 600 people, with homes and cars crushed by debris. Palm Beach's bishop dedicated Monday's All Souls' Day Mass to the nine victims.

The National Transportation Safety Board will now work to establish a cause, a process that typically takes months. Weather, the crew's decisions, and the jet's own recorders and maintenance history will all be part of that inquiry.

items.title: Justice Department to send more than 1,000 election monitors to polls in all 50 states
items.summary:
The Justice Department is dramatically expanding its Election Day monitoring this year, sending more than 1,000 federal monitors to polling places across all 50 states for Tuesday's midterms. That is a major increase from the 2022 midterms, when observers went to 64 jurisdictions in 24 states.

Some local officials said they received little explanation for why their area was selected. Several noted their jurisdictions are liberal-leaning places with large Hispanic populations. In North Dakota's Cass County, officials said a handful of monitors would visit up to seven polling sites for about an hour each to observe compliance with federal election law, and that monitors may not interact with voters near a polling place.

Voting-rights groups, including the NAACP, argue a large federal presence could discourage some voters and have sued to block the use of law enforcement agents as monitors. A court hearing in that challenge was scheduled for Monday afternoon. The department says its monitors only observe and document possible violations of federal voting law.

Watch the hearing outcome and Tuesday's actual deployments. Disputes over where monitors can stand inside or outside polling places could become an early flashpoint on Election Day itself.

items.title: Voters head into the midterms in a sour mood on prices, even as jobs and growth look solid
items.summary:
On the eve of an election that will decide control of Congress, many voters are focused less on headline economic strength and more on what daily life costs. Reuters reporting Monday described voters blaming tariffs and the Iran war for persistent inflation, with prices at the gas pump, on utility bills and at restaurants shaping how people feel about the economy.

The underlying numbers are mixed, not disastrous. Unemployment was 4.2% in September and has stayed at or below 4.5% for five straight years, weekly jobless claims are near a 57-year low, and the economy grew at a 3.4% annual pace last quarter, its strongest showing this year. One consumer confidence measure improved in October, even as a separate sentiment measure sat near a record low.

The gap between those two views helps explain the politics. Pay and prices have both risen about 5.5% since January 2025, leaving typical workers roughly even in purchasing power, while mortgage rates above 7% and a shortage of homes keep buying a house out of reach for many. The Federal Reserve raised rates in September and is expected to do so again in December.

That mix — a stable job market that still feels unaffordable — is the economic backdrop both parties must answer for on Tuesday, and it will outlast the election for whoever wins Congress.

items.title: South Florida soaked again Monday: flood watch, closed schools, and streets underwater
items.summary:
Much of South and Central Florida spent Monday under water or watching it rise, as torrential downpours continued for another day. All of South Florida is under a flood watch through Monday evening, with the National Weather Service expecting another one to three inches of rain and up to nine inches possible in isolated spots, raising the risk of rapid flash flooding.

The immediate warnings were already firing at midday. A flash flood warning covered parts of St. Lucie County until early afternoon after four to eight inches had already fallen, with two to four more inches possible. Brevard County closed its schools for the day, surf crashed over sea walls, and waves reached as high as 15 feet with gusts near 50 mph.

Local services are straining under the water. Cocoa Beach reduced trash pickup, closed recreational facilities, and asked residents to conserve water because heavy rainfall is overwhelming the city's wastewater system. Streets and highways across the region have become impassable in places.

Forecasters tie the deluge to a stack of factors at once: normal autumn rain, high-tide flooding, a closer-than-usual full moon last week, and a low-pressure area over the Bahamas interacting with high pressure over the Mid-Atlantic. Watch whether the rain finally eases tonight, as the flood watch currently suggests.

items.title: Trump makes his closing midterm pitch at the Reflecting Pool, with approval at a pre-midterm low
items.summary:
President Trump was set to deliver his closing message of the midterm campaign on Monday afternoon at the Reflecting Pool in Washington, capping a blitz of last-minute appearances in states where Republicans face competitive challengers. Tuesday's elections will determine who controls Congress for Trump's final two years in office, with his agenda hinging on a handful of key contests.

He makes that pitch from a weak polling position. Trump's approval rating stands at 36%, with 61% disapproving, according to the New York Times poll tracker — described in USA Today's coverage as the lowest approval for any president heading into a midterm election in the last 80 years. The Times' final national poll with Siena University linked the falling favorability to several of voters' top issues.

The weekend before the speech only added turbulence, including the unexpected cross-party endorsement in Michigan's Senate race that sent shockwaves through battleground contests. A federal judge also dismissed a Trump administration lawsuit in Alaska's closely watched Senate races over the weekend.

Whether a presidential closing argument can move late-deciding voters in individual House and Senate races is the open question. The answer starts arriving when polls close Tuesday night.

items.title: Energy drinks and stimulant supplements show up far more often in reports of serious heart events in young adults
items.summary:
New preliminary research released Monday found that caffeinated energy drinks and stimulant supplements appeared disproportionately in federal reports of serious heart problems, especially among adults ages 18 to 34. The findings, based on Food and Drug Administration adverse-event reports, are to be presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions later this week in Chicago.

Researchers reviewed more than 28,000 reports from 2017 through 2025, including 854 involving products with caffeine or other stimulants. Cardiac arrest was reported about 11 times more often in connection with those products than with products without stimulants. Heart attacks were reported about 4.5 times more often, and abnormal rhythms in the heart's lower chambers and palpitations about four times more often. About 45% of the stimulant-linked cardiovascular reports involved people ages 18 to 34.

The authors and heart experts stress what the study does not show. These are voluntary reports, so the analysis can show a pattern in reported events but cannot prove the products caused them, and it cannot show how many people used the products with no problem. The work has not yet been peer-reviewed. A separate 2026 Heart Association statement says up to 400 milligrams of caffeine a day is generally safe for most adults.

Watch for peer review and any follow-up research that can measure actual risk, including whether use before intense exercise, mixing with alcohol, or an undiagnosed heart condition explains part of the pattern.

items.title: Ohio smashes its midterm early-voting record before Election Day
items.summary:
More than 1.7 million Ohioans had already cast ballots ahead of Tuesday's Nov. 3 election, setting a new record for early voting in a midterm in the state.

Nearly 1.1 million people voted in person through Nov. 1, the last day of early voting, and about 632,000 mail ballots had been returned, according to figures from the Ohio secretary of state cited in the report. More than 104,000 absentee ballots were still outstanding, and those must be back by 7:30 p.m. on Election Day to count. The new total passed the previous midterm early-voting mark of 1.5 million set in 2022.

The shift was not simply more voting overall — it was a shift in how people voted. Far fewer Ohioans chose mail ballots this year, with 736,733 absentee ballots issued compared with roughly 1 million requested four years ago. Election officials and analysts pointed to heavy advertising and heightened interest, along with unease about mail delivery after national debate over the mail system.

Unaffiliated voters were the largest group in the early vote, with 887,372 ballots issued and 806,704 returned, ahead of registered Democrats and Republicans in raw numbers. That makes the early totals hard to read as a partisan forecast: the people who have already voted include a huge bloc whose preferences are not tied to a party label, and Tuesday's in-person vote still has to be counted.

items.title: Don't mail it now: Ohio mail ballots must arrive by 7:30 p.m. Tuesday
items.summary:
With early in-person voting over, Ohioans who still hold a mail ballot are being urged to drop it off in person rather than risk it arriving late.

Under Senate Bill 293, signed by Gov. Mike DeWine in December 2025, most absentee ballots must reach the local board of elections by the close of polls on Election Day, 7:30 p.m. on Nov. 3, to be counted. The old four-day grace period for ballots arriving after Election Day is gone, with an exception for military and overseas voters.

Secretary of State Frank LaRose said on Oct. 27 that it might already be too late to mail a ballot and have it arrive in time, according to Cleveland.com reporting cited in the guide. The practical advice is therefore to use a board of elections drop-off location instead of a mailbox.

For Cuyahoga County voters, that drop-off is the Board of Elections at 1803 Superior Ave. in Cleveland. The same 7:30 p.m. Tuesday deadline applies to Election Day polling places, which are open from 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.

items.title: Cavs list Watson as questionable for tonight's Thunder game
items.summary:
The Cavaliers released a five-player injury report for Monday night's home game against Oklahoma City, with guard Peyton Watson listed as questionable because of right hamstring tightness and soreness.

Watson has not missed a game this season, but the team is expected to be careful given that he dealt with two separate right hamstring strains last season. Jaylon Tyson is out with a right ankle sprain after missing the win at Milwaukee, and Nae'Qwan Tomlin is out with a low back stress reaction diagnosed before the season, with a possible return later in November.

Both teams enter the game at 4-2, but they are heading in opposite directions. Cleveland is 3-0 at home and coming off a 136-111 rout at Milwaukee, while Oklahoma City has lost two straight and is missing several key players, including Chet Holmgren, Jalen Williams, Cason Wallace and Alex Caruso.

The matchup still centers on the star guards, with Donovan Mitchell leading Cleveland against two-time reigning MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. If Watson cannot go, Cleveland's perimeter defense takes a hit against a Thunder team that, even short-handed, can lean on Gilgeous-Alexander to create offense.

items.title: Watson says he is fine after concussion check in Pittsburgh loss
items.summary:
Browns quarterback Deshaun Watson said he was OK after a first-quarter hit sent him to the medical tent for a concussion evaluation during Sunday's 27-6 loss at Pittsburgh.

Watson took a hit from Steelers safety Jaquan Brisker just over five minutes into the game, was flagged for roughing the passer on the play, and left for the evaluation while Shedeur Sanders finished the series. Watson cleared the check, returned, and finished 27-of-39 for 324 yards with no touchdowns, while being sacked eight times, tying a season high.

After the game Watson described the sideline check as standard league protocol and said the brain is one of the body's most important organs, so the evaluation had to happen. He also took responsibility for some of the sacks, saying he needed to get the ball out faster and use his checkdowns instead of trying to extend plays.

The loss dropped Cleveland to 5-3 and third in the AFC North, behind Pittsburgh at 6-2, and the Browns now turn to a road game at New Orleans on Sunday. How well the offensive line protects Watson, and how quickly he gets rid of the ball, will be the immediate question after a game in which Pittsburgh's rush controlled the afternoon.

items.title: Judge strikes down extra hurdle for Medicaid disability exemptions
items.summary:
A federal judge has thrown out a Trump administration requirement that would have forced many people with disabilities to prove they cannot work in order to keep Medicaid coverage under new work rules.

Starting next year, most state Medicaid programs must run so-called community engagement rules, under which beneficiaries generally must show at least 80 hours a month of work, volunteering or school to qualify. Congress said people who are medically frail or have special medical needs should be exempt, but a June rule from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services added a second test: the condition also had to significantly limit a person's ability to work.

Judge Richard Stearns, ruling late last week in a case brought by 25 states and Washington, D.C., found that extra limitation went beyond the agency's authority and ordered it removed, along with a six-month pause on enforcement of decisions about who counts as medically frail. Under the ruling, people need only show they fall into one of the five medically frail categories Congress set out.

Advocates called the decision a win for disabled people who might otherwise have lost coverage over paperwork, but they stressed that the Jan. 1 start date for the work rules has not changed. The Ohio Capital Journal also reported Nov. 2 that the American Medical Association, in a friend-of-the-court brief, warned the rule could threaten coverage for at least 140,000 Ohio Medicaid recipients — a reminder that the Ohio stakes in this national fight are large, and that documentation fights in the rule remain unresolved.

items.title: Cleveland Museum of Art opens new Jewish ceremonial art installation
items.summary:
The Cleveland Museum of Art has opened Furnishing American Synagogues: Jewish Ceremonial Art, a new installation of ritual objects on loan from the Jewish Museum in New York, on view from Nov. 1, 2026 through Oct. 24, 2027.

The works are shown in two of the museum's permanent collection galleries, 208 and 224A, and trace Jewish ritual life in the United States since the country's founding, timed to the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. Highlights include an early-1900s silver Torah crown, a contemporary mixed-media donation container, and a monumental Torah ark carved in 1899 by a Jewish immigrant for a synagogue in Sioux City, Iowa.

This is the third installation of Jewish ceremonial art from the Jewish Museum at Cleveland, building on the long working relationship between Cleveland director William Griswold and Jewish Museum director James Snyder. Rather than sitting in a separate Judaica gallery, the objects are placed among the museum's permanent collection, putting them in conversation with American art and daily life across centuries.

For Northeast Ohio visitors, the show is a free, long-running reason to return to University Circle: it runs for nearly a full year, so there is no rush to catch it in opening week, and its mix of historic craftsmanship and contemporary work gives families and first-time visitors an accessible entry point into both the museum and the history it tells.

baby.tip: Day two with a newborn: start a simple log on your phone — feed times, wet diapers and dirty diapers. It feels like overkill at 3 a.m., but the pediatrician's first questions at Benji's first visit (usually a few days after discharge) are exactly those counts, and nobody remembers them on no sleep. One shared note that both Mike and Kelly can add to beats two tired memories.
baby.fact: A newborn sees best at about 8 to 12 inches — almost exactly the distance between a feeding baby's face and a parent's face. Benji's vision is still blurry and he prefers high-contrast patterns and faces, which is why face-to-face time at feeding distance is, quite literally, his favorite view in the world right now.
baby.fun: Name tidbit for the day: Benjamin is a Hebrew name meaning 'son of the right hand,' and in the Bible Benjamin was the youngest of twelve brothers — a fitting name for the newest and youngest Smiley. Today's tiny mission: tell Benji the story of his name once, out loud, even if he sleeps through the whole thing.
